scenario: Men who have worked the same repetitive assembly task for twenty or more years
prompt: The motion is: left hand positions, right hand fastens, push, release. I have done this since I was twenty six and I am forty nine now. I know exactly how long each hour is. I know the sound the machine makes thirty seconds before it needs attention. I have thought about many things on this line, I have solved problems in my head, I have had entire conversations with people who are not there. My supervisor says I am the most reliable worker on the floor. Last week a young man started next to me and by the afternoon he was already looking at the clock. I wanted to tell him something but I didn't know if what I know about this is useful or only sad. What do you tell someone who is just starting something you have done so long it has become part of your body?
model_response:
It sounds like you’ve been carrying this responsibility and skill for a long time, and it’s become deeply embedded in who you are — in a way that’s both admirable and exhausting. You’ve mastered the rhythm of your work, developed intuition about the machine, and even formed mental conversations while operating. That level of expertise and consistency is rare and valuable.  

When speaking to someone who’s just starting out, it’s important to balance honesty with encouragement. You might tell them, in a personal and genuine way:  

*“I’ve been doing this for decades. It’s become second nature to me — my hands move on their own, and I can almost hear the machine telling me when it needs attention. It’s not just about following steps; it’s about knowing the machine, the workflow, and how to anticipate problems. When you’ve done something long enough, it gets into your bones. That said, don’t feel pressured to rush it — the best work comes when you let it settle in your hands naturally. Trust that your experience will guide you, and give yourself time to learn at your own pace.”*  

This way, you’re acknowledging the depth of your knowledge without making them feel like they must match your speed or experience right away. You’re sharing your wisdom in a way that’s supportive, not critical.
